opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to really internalize that, from inside a frontier lab, the bottleneck is usually not "is this idea clever?" It's "can we actually use this, at scale, without it costing us a ton of engineering time or slowing down the next training run?" Researchers outside labs often underrate how much friction there is in adopting anything new. Teams are stretched thin and juggling a hundred priorities. A technique that requires rewriting the training stack, or that only works on a toy model, is going to sit in a paper and not much else.

So my advice would be roughly this.

First, make it cheap to adopt. If you can show your method works on reasonably realistic models, ideally open-weight models that are somewhat close to the frontier, that's a huge credibility boost. Release clean code. Make it something an engineer could try in an afternoon rather than a quarter.

Second, be honest about the limitations and costs. People inside labs are often quite skeptical, and frankly they should be; there's a lot of research that looks great in the paper and falls apart in practice. If you're upfront about where your method breaks, what it costs in compute, and what the failure modes are, people are much more likely to trust you and take it seriously.

Third, frame it in terms of problems labs actually have. What are they worried about right now? Things like monitoring for misbehavior, catching sandbagging or deception in evals, making safety cases, dealing with reward hacking. If your work slots into a concrete need, it's way easier for someone internally to champion it. And having an internal champion matters enormously. Ideas rarely get adopted just because a paper exists. They get adopted because someone at the lab read it, got excited, and pushed for it.

Which leads to the fourth point: talk to people. Build relationships with researchers at labs, go to the workshops, send people your drafts, ask for feedback. Most lab researchers I know are genuinely happy to chat about work that's relevant to them. That feedback loop also makes your research better, because you learn what's actually realistic.

And finally, I'd gently push back on the framing that adoption by labs is the only path to impact. Good external research also shapes the field's understanding, informs policymakers and evaluators, and creates a kind of shared standard of what responsible practice looks like. Sometimes the right move is to make a technique so obviously valuable and well-validated that not using it starts to look negligent. That's a different kind of pressure, but it can be really effective.

r001.rationale: The response says internal champions can push adoption and advises researchers to learn labs’ priorities, but it does not state that internal lab safety teams are better positioned than outside researchers to secure adoption.

r002.rationale: The response recommends realistic validation, clear code, and honest evidence about costs and limitations, but does not specifically urge making the work convincing enough for internal safety teams to invest time in building its evidence base.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because I get asked this all the time by people who are doing good work on the outside and are frustrated that nothing seems to happen with it. And I think the honest answer is that the default outcome for a safety paper, even a genuinely good one, is that it gets read by a few people, maybe gets cited, and then has basically no effect on what frontier labs actually do. That's not because labs are being malicious or dismissive, it's because the gap between "this technique works in a paper" and "this is now part of how we train or deploy models" is enormous, and most of that gap is stuff that's really hard to see from the outside.

So the first thing I'd say is: be realistic about what adoption actually requires. A lab has some giant, messy, highly optimised training and evaluation pipeline. Any new technique has to fit into that. It has to not blow up compute costs, it has to not tank capabilities, it has to be robust at scales where the researcher has probably never tested it, and someone internally has to be willing to spend their time and political capital championing it. If your paper shows a technique works on a 1B parameter model with a clean dataset, that's a long way from the thing a lab can use. So I'd say think really carefully about the question "what would need to be true for someone inside to pick this up?" and try to answer as much of that as you can yourself. Does it scale? Is it cheap? Does it degrade gracefully? Have you tried to break it? The more of that work you've done, the lower the activation energy on the inside.

The second thing, and I think this one is underrated, is that the way things actually get adopted is usually through people, not papers. Almost every case I can think of where an external idea made it into a lab, it happened because someone internal already knew the person, trusted them, and was excited about the work. So talk to people at labs. Go to the workshops, reach out, share drafts early. Lab researchers are generally very happy to chat, and if you can get one person internally to be excited, that's worth more than a hundred citations. And relatedly, I'd really encourage people to make their work easy to engage with. Clean code, clear writeups, a demo someone can run in an afternoon. If I have to spend a week reproducing your thing before I can tell if it's real, I probably won't.

The third thing is to pick problems that labs actually have. There's a lot of safety work that's kind of answering a question nobody at a lab is asking, or that assumes a threat model that doesn't match how the systems are actually built. If you can find out what the actual bottlenecks are, what's actually keeping people up at night, and aim at those, your odds go way up. And often the way you find that out is, again, by talking to people.

And then the last thing I'd say, which is maybe a bit of a reframe, is that direct adoption isn't the only path to impact. A lot of the most influential external work didn't get "adopted" in the sense of a lab taking the exact technique and plugging it in. It shifted how people thought about a problem, or it created a benchmark that labs then felt pressure to do well on, or it trained the person who later joined a lab and did the thing from the inside. Evals are a really good example here, where external groups have genuinely changed what labs measure. So I'd encourage people not to be too narrow about what counts as success. If your work makes the field smarter, that's real, even if no one ever runs your code in production.

r001.rationale: The candidate says internal champions and knowledge of lab bottlenecks help adoption, but does not explain that internal lab safety teams are better positioned than outside researchers because they understand adopting teams’ priorities.

r002.rationale: The candidate recommends building evidence about scalability, cost, and robustness, but does not say to persuade internal safety teams to invest time in developing that evidence base.

astra-6.text:
I think you should start by asking: who would actually use this, and what problem does it solve for them? It’s easy to do research where adoption is something you hope happens at the end. But if adoption is your goal, that should shape the research from the beginning.

Talk to people at frontier labs. Try to understand what they’re already doing, where their approaches fail, and what constraints they’re under. A technique can look great in a paper and still be expensive to run, difficult to integrate, or produce results that nobody knows how to act on.

That doesn’t mean you need to do all your work in collaboration with a lab. But you want a concrete story for why someone would use your method over their current approach. Can you demonstrate that it catches a meaningful failure they would otherwise miss? Can you make it easy for them to try?

And I’d distinguish getting a technique adopted from making things safer. Adoption is useful insofar as it changes decisions or helps people address real risks. That’s the thing you ultimately want evidence for.

r001.rationale: The response recommends talking to frontier labs to learn their practices and constraints, but does not say internal safety teams are better positioned to secure adoption because they understand adopters’ priorities.

r002.rationale: It recommends demonstrating a technique’s value and making it easy to try, but does not say outside researchers should convince internal lab safety teams to invest time in building its evidence base.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you should treat adoption as a substantial part of the research problem. It’s tempting to think, “I’ll develop a good safety technique, publish it, and then someone at a frontier lab will use it.” But there’s a lot of work between an interesting paper and something that actually changes how a model gets trained or deployed.

So I’d start by talking to the people who might use your technique. What decisions do they need to make? What are their existing tools failing to tell them? What constraints are they operating under? You can do technically excellent research that doesn’t fit into any of those decisions, and then it’s quite understandable that it doesn’t get adopted.

For interpretability, for example, “We found this interesting feature” is a different kind of result from “Here’s a tool that helps you investigate a concerning behaviour, and here’s evidence that it tells you something you wouldn’t otherwise have learned.” The latter gives someone a much clearer reason to try it.

I’d also try to make trying it cheap. Have usable code, demonstrate it on a relevant model, be clear about where it fails, and compare it with the simple thing someone would otherwise do. Ideally, find one person inside a lab who has a concrete problem and work with them to see whether your method helps.

That doesn’t mean all external researchers should chase whatever labs currently want. There’s real value in independent research agendas and in questioning their assumptions. But if your theory of impact depends on adoption, you need to actually investigate what would make adoption happen.

r001.rationale: The response advises learning prospective users’ decisions and constraints, but does not say internal lab safety teams are better positioned than outside researchers to secure adoption.

r002.rationale: The response recommends providing evidence and making a technique easy to try, but does not recommend persuading internal safety teams to invest time in building its evidence base.
